lane.name: Cosmic country and the '70s revival
lane.definition: Grateful Dead-, Gram Parsons- and Laurel Canyon-indebted guitar bands and songwriters: buttery lead guitar, harmonies, breezy tempos, long instrumental passages.

albums.label: Birdman Records
albums.description: Howlin Rain's debut is a cult favorite of thick, fuzzed-out Crazy Horse-style guitar rock, Ethan Miller's voice straining over extended riffing that owes as much to the Allman Brothers as to Neil Young. It set up the heavier, more maximalist sound Miller would carry through the American Recordings years.
albums.lineage: Ethan Miller's move from the noisier Comets on Fire into a more classic-rock sound that is indebted to Crazy Horse and the Allman Brothers, launching his long-running Howlin Rain project.

albums.label: Woodsist
albums.description: Woods' scrappy early album is home-taped campfire folk buried in tape hiss, with Jeremy Earl's high, cracked voice floating over acoustic strums and found-sound collage. It is one of the rawest documents of the Woodsist label's early lo-fi, backyard-show aesthetic.
albums.lineage: An early Woods/Woodsist record, cut from the same DIY-cassette cloth as Earl's early-2000s Brooklyn basement-show scene.

albums.label: American Recordings
albums.description: Ethan Miller's band follows up their debut with a bigger record of heavy, extended guitar jams built on Crazy Horse-style fuzz and Southern-rock swagger. Songs stretch out into long instrumental sections without losing their anthemic hooks. It suits listeners who want 1970s-scaled hard rock with room to roam.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to Neil Young & Crazy Horse and the Allman Brothers' long jams; Miller came from the psych band Comets on Fire.
key_tracks: Dancers at the End of Time

albums.label: Secretly Canadian
albums.description: Adam Granduciel's full-length debut with the band, a hazy blend of Dylan-style harmonica and drawl with Crazy Horse guitar sprawl. Long, meandering tracks like 'Buenos Aires Beach' stretch toward Americana psychedelia rather than pop songcraft. It is for listeners who want the roots of the band's later widescreen sound in a rawer, more ragged form.
albums.lineage: The band was co-founded in Philadelphia by Granduciel and Kurt Vile; its harmonica-and-drawl sound is plainly indebted to Dylan and Neil Young, and it feeds into the more polished cosmic-Americana of the band's later records.

albums.label: Woodsist
albums.description: Denser and stranger than the debut, this record piles tape-collage noise interludes between fragile folk songs, sketching the push-pull between prettiness and racket that would define the band. Earl's warbling falsetto is already fully formed here.
albums.lineage: Deepens the lo-fi Woodsist-scene template before the band's melodies sharpened on Songs of Shame.

albums.album: Flash Forward to the Good Times
albums.label: Kemado Records
albums.description: The former Beachwood Sparks multi-instrumentalist's solo debut is loose, sun-baked country-psych, heavy on steel guitar and warm analog fuzz. It sounds like an extension of the same Laurel Canyon-revival scene he helped build in his band work.
albums.lineage: A solo outlet for a Beachwood Sparks member, carrying that band's 2000s LA cosmic-country revival sound into looser, more psychedelic territory.
key_tracks: Flash Forward to the Good Times

albums.label: Woodsist
albums.description: Jeremy Earl's Brooklyn band moves from bedroom-folk haze to a fuller, live-sounding record, with G. Lucas Crane's cassette collages woven through. Earl's falsetto floats over fuzzy, Crazy Horse-style guitar runs and Kraut-rock-tinged jams. A defining record of the late-2000s Woodsist/DIY scene.
albums.lineage: Grew out of Earl's early lo-fi cassette recordings and the Woodsist label he runs; its sunny psych-folk and guitar jams sound indebted to Neil Young and 1960s psych-folk.

albums.label: Woodsist
albums.description: The follow-up to Songs of Shame leans further into sun-soaked pop hooks while keeping the tape-hiss production and Earl's high, reedy voice. Crane's found-sound collage and fuzzy guitar keep it from ever feeling too straightforward. A quintessential entry in the Woodsist label's back catalog, for fans of short, hazy psych-folk songs.
albums.lineage: Continues directly from Songs of Shame's DIY tape production, with guitar sprawl that sounds indebted to Crazy Horse.

albums.label: Domino
albums.description: Released the same year as Wit's End as its looser, funnier counterpart, Humor Risk swaps that record's hush for jangling guitar-pop and McCombs' driest deadpan wit. It's one of his most purely enjoyable, least somber records.
albums.lineage: The comic flip side to Wit's End within McCombs' prolific Domino years, sounding closer to the Drag City deadpan tradition than his more mournful work.

albums.label: Bella Union
albums.description: Wilson's breakout solo album is a sprawling, hour-long homage to Laurel Canyon songwriting, built on layered acoustic and pedal-steel textures and long, patient guitar passages. Recorded in his own Laurel Canyon studio, it openly revives the Crosby, Stills & Nash and Neil Young sound of the neighborhood's golden age. It suits listeners who want slow-burning, lushly harmonized folk rock.
albums.lineage: Sounds like a conscious recreation of the Laurel Canyon country-rock of CSNY and Neil Young, made in the same neighborhood that produced it.

albums.label: Secretly Canadian
albums.description: The War on Drugs' second album layers motorik drum-machine pulse under harmonica, slide guitar and reverb-soaked vocals, moving toward the widescreen sound the band would perfect later. Tracks bleed into one another like a long highway drive, closer to Springsteen-via-Eno than jam-band twang. A transitional record between the group's scrappier debut and its arena-ready future.
albums.lineage: Bridges the band's Crazy Horse-inflected debut and the fully formed synth-Americana of Lost in the Dream, sounding indebted to Springsteen and Eno-style ambience.

albums.label: Woodsist
albums.description: Woods stretch out further here, with side-long instrumental jams sitting next to their usual sun-dappled pop songs. It is the most explicitly Dead-indebted record in their catalog to that point, trading some of the earlier tape-hiss murk for cleaner, more expansive guitar interplay.
albums.lineage: Marks the band's turn toward longer, more overtly jam-based arrangements, anticipating Bend Beyond and the band's live reputation.

albums.label: Sub Pop
albums.description: A reunion album made squarely within the 2010s cosmic-country revival scene they'd predicted a decade earlier, The Tarnished Gold sounds warmer and more relaxed than the debut without losing its pedal-steel-heavy Parsons worship. It plays like a welcome-home record for a band whose sound had finally caught up with everyone else.
albums.lineage: Beachwood Sparks returning to their Gram Parsons-descended sound at a moment when bands like Woods were working a similar Parsons/Dead vein, a parallel rather than a direct link.

albums.label: Captured Tracks
albums.description: Cohen's solo debut after Deerhoof and the Curtains sets warped, subdued psychedelic pop against loose, home-recorded arrangements. Guitars ring and drift rather than solo, and the tempos stay unhurried throughout. It established the mysterious, hazy sound that runs through his later solo work.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to breezy Laurel Canyon-style pop songwriting, filtered through a lo-fi, tape-warped production sensibility.

albums.label: American Recordings
albums.description: A dense, heavily produced record of sprawling, riff-driven rock songs, several stretching past seven minutes with extended guitar interplay. It leans harder into arena-scaled classic rock than Howlin Rain's earlier records, while keeping the same Dead- and Crazy Horse-indebted jam structure. It suits listeners who want big, road-worn guitar rock.
albums.lineage: Pushes Magnificent Fiend's long-jam sound, which sounds indebted to Crazy Horse and Southern rock, toward a heavier, more maximalist studio production.

albums.label: Woodsist
albums.description: Bend Beyond captures the muscular, Crazy Horse-inflected live sound the band had built over years of touring, with cleaner production than their tape-hiss records. Harmonized guitars and Earl's falsetto ride anthemic, sun-dappled melodies. A high point of the band's Woodsist-era run.
albums.lineage: The culmination of the band's 2009-2012 Woodsist run, after which they continued to evolve toward more polished psych-pop on later albums.

albums.label: Domino
albums.description: A sprawling double album that runs from lean country-rock to hazier, longer jams, Big Wheel and Others is McCombs at his most expansive and least predictable. Its length and range make it feel like a summation of everything he'd tried across the previous decade.
albums.lineage: A career-spanning-feeling double LP that pulls together McCombs' country-rock, folk and jam tendencies before his tighter ANTI- Records period.

albums.artist: Chris Forsyth & the Solar Motel Band
albums.label: Paradise of Bachelors
albums.description: A four-part instrumental suite that moves from Garcia-like lead lines into denser, noisier electric passages, Solar Motel is Forsyth's move from solo-guitar Primitivism toward full-band, jam-length rock. It's less a set of songs than a single continuous guitar exploration, for listeners who like patient, building instrumental rock.
albums.lineage: Forsyth's crossover from the American Primitive solo-guitar world into full-band Dead- and Television-indebted jamming, launching the Solar Motel Band.

albums.label: Bella Union
albums.description: A denser, more orchestrated follow-up to Gentle Spirit, adding strings and a wide cast of guests to Wilson's long-form country-rock songs. Extended guitar jams and layered harmonies stretch several tracks well past the six-minute mark. It suits listeners who want maximal, immersive 1970s-style studio rock.
albums.lineage: Expands Gentle Spirit's guitar rock, which sounds indebted to Laurel Canyon and the Grateful Dead, into a more maximalist, string-laden record.

albums.label: Woodsist
albums.description: Morby's solo debut is a hushed, meandering set cut loose from Woods' bass-and-harmony pop, built on repeated guitar figures, mumbled Dylan-indebted phrasing, and a side-long title track that stretches past nine minutes. It set the template of unhurried, half-lit songwriting he'd refine for a decade.
albums.lineage: Grew directly out of Morby's time as Woods' bassist and the Woodsist label scene; its hypnotic, Crazy Horse/Velvets-like drone carries forward into his solo run.

albums.label: Paradise of Bachelors
albums.description: One of the first Gunn albums to put his own singing at the front alongside his guitar playing, Time Off pairs raga-like fingerpicked figures with a laconic, half-sung drawl. It reads as the turning point where his American Primitive guitar background became actual songs.
albums.lineage: Steve Gunn crosses over from the solo-guitar American Primitive lineage into full band-and-vocal cosmic country, a move he'd deepen on Way Out Weather.

albums.label: Sacred Bones
albums.description: Damon McMahon's Amen Dunes trades earlier lo-fi murk for warmer, more melodic songs built on loping acoustic guitar and a breathy, drawling voice. Tempos stay slow and breezy, closer to hazy folk-rock than to the drone of his earlier records. It suits listeners who like hypnotic, devotional-sounding songs that unfold slowly.
albums.lineage: Moves Amen Dunes toward a hazier guitar-folk sound that sounds indebted to classic rock and Gram Parsons-era country rock.

albums.artist: Chris Forsyth & the Solar Motel Band
albums.label: No Quarter
albums.description: The Solar Motel Band's breakthrough tightens Forsyth's guitar suites into denser, riff-driven pieces, still stretching well past the length of a normal rock song. Interlocking electric leads and a steady rhythm section make it the most direct entry point into his band work.
albums.lineage: The full-band follow-up to Solar Motel, carrying Forsyth's Television- and Dead-indebted guitar vocabulary into tighter, riff-driven pieces.

albums.label: Merge
albums.description: M.C. Taylor's first Merge album loosens the ragged folk of his earlier records into warmer, full-band arrangements with pedal steel and organ. The songs move at an unhurried, breezy pace, with Taylor's rasp working through themes of family and faith. It is the record that carried Hiss Golden Messenger out of the private-press underground and into a wider Americana audience.
albums.lineage: Grows out of the raw, homemade folk of Bad Debt and Haw into a fuller country-rock sound that sounds indebted to the Grateful Dead and the Band, which Taylor kept refining on later Merge albums.
key_tracks: Lord, Help The Poor and Needy

albums.label: Woodsist
albums.description: Morby's second solo LP tightens the songs from Harlem River into brisker, more country-inflected shapes, trading some of the drone for clearer verse-chorus structures and road-worn narrative detail. It's still recognizably Woodsist-scene lo-fi, but pointed toward the widescreen songwriting of his Dead Oceans records.
albums.lineage: A bridge between Morby's Woods/Woodsist roots and the more polished, Dead Oceans-era songwriter he'd become on Singing Saw.

albums.label: Paradise of Bachelors
albums.description: A full-band leap forward from Time Off, with a rhythm section giving Gunn's winding guitar lines somewhere to breathe and his voice settling into an easy, sun-warmed drawl. Its interlocking guitars recall both Television and the Grateful Dead. It suits listeners who like long, rolling guitar songs.
albums.lineage: Consolidates Gunn's move from solo-guitar Primitivism into a proper cosmic-country band sound, setting up his run on Matador.

albums.label: Secretly Canadian
albums.description: The band's breakthrough: widescreen, synth-lined heartland rock with long, patient builds, pedal-steel-like guitar figures and Granduciel's plainspoken, hurting voice. Motorik drums and layered guitars keep songs rolling for seven or eight minutes at a time. It suits late-night drivers and anyone who wants anxiety turned into slow-burning catharsis.
albums.lineage: Sounds descended from Dylan, Petty and Springsteen filtered through Eno-style production; its widescreen sound echoes in later bands like Wild Pink and Hovvdy.

albums.label: Woodsist
albums.description: Woods' sound had fully bloomed into warm, jammy classic-rock by this point, with the nine-minute title track stretching into extended guitar interplay reminiscent of the Dead and the Allmans. Earl's falsetto now floats over full-band arrangements rather than tape hiss.
albums.lineage: Marks Woods' full transition from lo-fi folk to the jam-friendly cosmic country sound that runs through the rest of their catalog and the wider Woodsist scene.

albums.label: Silver Current Records
albums.description: A looser, more organic-sounding record than The Russian Wilds, leaning into warmer, more soulful arrangements. Extended guitar solos still anchor several songs, but the overall feel is breezier and less studio-heavy. It suits listeners who like classic-rock sprawl with a gentler, homespun touch.
albums.lineage: Returns Howlin Rain's jamming, which sounds indebted to Crazy Horse and the Dead, to a rawer, band-in-a-room feel after the maximalism of The Russian Wilds.

albums.label: Paradise of Bachelors
albums.description: A young Nashville band's second album, expanding from garage-country burners into ambitious, Byrds- and Big Star-indebted psych-country. Twin guitars, ringing harmonies and long instrumental stretches give it a loose, '70s feel. It suits listeners who like cosmic country with a bit of rock-and-roll grit.
albums.lineage: Released by Paradise of Bachelors, tying it to that label's American-vernacular roster; the sound is indebted to the Byrds and Big Star.

albums.label: Dead Oceans
albums.description: Walker's breakthrough backs his fingerpicked-guitar songwriting with Chicago jazz and experimental players, stretching folk songs into loose, Van Morrison- and Tim Buckley-indebted jams. It is warm, exploratory and unhurried, for listeners who like folk that drifts toward improvisation.
albums.lineage: Pulls jazz improvisation into a folk-rock frame that sounds indebted to Astral Weeks and the Grateful Dead's more pastoral side.

albums.label: Sub Pop
albums.description: Georgia punks turned Dead-worshipping jammers, Arbor Labor Union's Sub Pop debut is fuzzed-out, repetitive guitar rock that treats a single riff as a launchpad for extended noise. It's the loudest, most distortion-caked branch of the cosmic-country revival covered here.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to Meat Puppets' punk-bred psychedelia and the Dead's long-form jamming, pushed toward drone and distortion.

albums.label: ANTI-
albums.description: McCombs' ANTI- debut loosens his usual cryptic songwriting into warm, soulful, mid-tempo arrangements with breezy electric-guitar interplay and light horns. It is one of his most accessible records, closer to yacht-rock smoothness than to the noisier turns of his earlier catalog. Political and personal songs sit side by side without ever raising their voice.
albums.lineage: Pulls McCombs' idiosyncratic songwriting toward a breezier guitar-rock sound that sounds indebted to the Grateful Dead and continues on Tip of the Sphere and Heartmind.

albums.label: Captured Tracks
albums.description: A slightly warmer, more melodic follow-up to Overgrown Path, keeping Cohen's soft-focus psychedelic pop but adding more overt hooks and clearer vocal lines. Tempos remain breezy and the mood mellow throughout. It continues his run of quietly beloved, low-key solo records.
albums.lineage: Refines the hazy, Laurel Canyon-adjacent pop songwriting of Overgrown Path without changing course.

albums.label: Drag City
albums.description: Hanson's first solo album away from his fuzzed-out band Wand strips things back to gentle, string-and-pedal-steel-laced folk-rock, closer to Gene Clark than to Wand's noise. His high, plaintive voice sits up front over patient, breezy arrangements. It is a quiet detour from the guitar heroics of his main band.
albums.lineage: Moves Hanson from Wand's psych-fuzz toward a hushed country-folk sound that sounds indebted to Gene Clark and Laurel Canyon, which resurfaces in his later solo work.

albums.label: Merge
albums.description: M.C. Taylor turns worries about work, fatherhood, and getting by into some of his most direct, tuneful songwriting, backed by a road-tested band playing loose, breezy country-soul. Pedal steel, warm harmonies, and rolling grooves carry the songs, sitting between Southern soul and country rock. It suits listeners who want comforting, grown-up roots music with a bit of swing.
albums.lineage: Continues the country-soul direction of Lateness of Dancers; its loose, communal grooves sound indebted to the Band and the Grateful Dead.
key_tracks: Like a Mirror Loves a Hammer

albums.label: Brutal Honest
albums.description: Williamson's second album on her own vanity label is sparser and more intimate than her later Mexican Summer records, built on fingerpicked guitar and a plainspoken alto working through heartbreak and searching. It's the clearest link between her early Texas-folk sound and the cosmic-country turn of Cosmic Wink.
albums.lineage: A self-released bridge between Williamson's Native State debut and her Mexican Summer albums, still close to Texas singer-songwriter tradition.

albums.label: Dead Oceans
albums.description: Morby's first album for Dead Oceans opens his sound way up, with a full band, strings and pedal steel behind songs written after his move from New York to Los Angeles. The looping, piano-led title track is the clearest signal yet of his Laurel Canyon leanings. It suits listeners who like slow-burning, widescreen singer-songwriter rock.
albums.lineage: Morby's turn from home-recorded folk toward orchestrated songwriting that sounds indebted to Gram Parsons and Laurel Canyon, setting up City Music and the rest of his Dead Oceans run.
key_tracks: I Have Been to the Mountain

albums.album: Golden Sings That Have Been Sung
albums.label: Dead Oceans
albums.description: A deliberate evolution from Primrose Green's jazz-folk sprawl toward tighter, more song-focused arrangements, still built on Walker's intricate guitar work and a loose, breezy band feel. The mood is hushed and exploratory, another turn in his continually shifting sound.
albums.lineage: The second of Walker's Dead Oceans albums, part of his restless movement between folk, jazz and rock idioms.

albums.label: Saddle Creek
albums.description: Sam Owens' debut as Sam Evian is a warm, lightly psychedelic bedroom-folk record, its analog haze pointing toward the Flying Cloud studio he'd later build with Hannah Cohen. Soft-focus vocals, round bass and loose drums make it a gentle, sunlit listen for fans of '70s-inflected home recording.
albums.lineage: The starting point for the Flying Cloud/Hannah Cohen upstate-New York recording circle Evian would go on to anchor as a producer.

albums.label: Matador
albums.description: Gunn's Matador debut sharpens his songwriting into tighter, more rock-band arrangements while keeping the long instrumental release valves. Touring and travel are all over the lyrics, matching the record's road-worn, motorik-tinged guitar interplay.
albums.lineage: First album for Matador Records, broadening Gunn's audience beyond the Paradise of Bachelors underground while keeping the same guitar-forward songwriting.

albums.label: Secretly Canadian
albums.description: Formed from the ashes of Smith Westerns, Whitney's debut pairs Julien Ehrlich's high falsetto with warm horn charts and loose, country-tinged guitar picking, closer to the Band's easy soulfulness than to jam-band sprawl. It became a defining record of mid-2010s soft, horn-driven indie rock.
albums.lineage: Grew out of the collapse of Smith Westerns' glammy power-pop into a gentler, horn-and-pedal-steel-inflected country-soul sound.

albums.album: City Sun Eater in the River of Light
albums.label: Woodsist
albums.description: Woods add horns and a looser, more percussive groove here, leaning into dub and Afrobeat-tinged rhythm sections under their usual searching guitar solos. It's the most rhythmically adventurous entry in a catalog otherwise built on jangle and drone.
albums.lineage: Pushes the Woodsist-scene sound outward from straight cosmic-country jamming toward polyrhythmic, horn-inflected arrangements.

albums.label: Salinas Records
albums.description: Bonny Doon's debut is a gentle, unhurried collection of plainspoken country-folk songs built on loping tempos and warm, conversational vocal harmonies between Bill Lennox and Bobby Colombo. It's understated where their later records get looser and more rock-facing. It's for fans of hushed, front-porch songwriting.
albums.lineage: Grows out of Detroit's indie scene (with ties to Waxahatchee, whose Saint Cloud the band would later back); sets up the more Woodsist-style slacker sound of Longwave.

albums.label: Merge
albums.description: A joyful counterpart to Heart Like a Levee's worry, leaning into gospel-tinged uplift and a live-in-the-room band feel. The guitars are warm and interlocked, with less studio polish and loose, rolling tempos. Its songs about hard times and gratitude suit fans of communal, soulful country rock.
albums.lineage: Keeps Hiss Golden Messenger's cosmic-country sound loose and communal; the road-band feel sounds indebted to the Grateful Dead and the Band.

albums.label: New West Records
albums.description: Produced by Jeff Tweedy, this album pairs the Saskatchewan cousins' antique folk repertoire and close harmonies with warmer, more electric backing than their earlier records, edging toward a breezy country-rock feel. Clayton Linthicum's fingerpicked and occasionally fuzzed guitar work sits alongside Kacy Anderson's plain, unadorned voice. It suits listeners who like old-time song forms with a gentle rock pulse.
albums.lineage: Bridges Kacy & Clayton's traditional folk repertoire with producer Jeff Tweedy's fuller band arrangements, in a country-rock sound akin to Laurel Canyon.

albums.label: Dead Oceans
albums.description: Conceived as Singing Saw's noisier, city-set counterpart, City Music trades pastoral pedal steel for jangling electric guitars and long, driving jams. It is Morby's most explicitly Velvets- and Modern Lovers-indebted record, down to a brisk Ramones tribute in '1234', while still carrying his country-rock phrasing.
albums.lineage: The urban mirror to Singing Saw's rural songs, sounding more directly indebted to the Velvet Underground and Jonathan Richman, with an open Ramones homage.

albums.label: Spiritual Pajamas
albums.description: Clay Finch and Sam Blasucci's duo debut is built on intertwined nylon and steel-string acoustic guitars and close, easy harmonies, closer to Everly Brothers or Simon & Garfunkel than jam-band sprawl. It is unhurried, warm California folk-country, intimate rather than expansive.
albums.lineage: Sounds rooted in Everly-style duo harmony singing and 1970s California country rock.

albums.label: Atlantic
albums.description: The band's major-label debut pushes the sound even more polished and arena-scaled, with layered guitars and synth pads. It trades some of the earlier records' ragged charm for widescreen consistency, still built on long-form, slow-building songs. A record for driving at night with the windows down.
albums.lineage: Extends the cosmic-Americana approach of Lost in the Dream into a more maximalist, radio-scaled register.

albums.label: Tiny Engines
albums.description: Wild Pink's debut is a quiet, synth-tinged indie-rock record already reaching for the widescreen, heartland-adjacent atmosphere John Ross would refine on later albums. It's rougher and more DIY than the band's Royal Mountain-era work.
albums.lineage: The starting point of Wild Pink's catalog, before their sound expanded into the fuller heartland-indie of A Billion Little Lights.

albums.label: Woodsist
albums.description: Written fast in the aftermath of the 2016 election, this is a quieter, more direct record than its predecessors, trading the horn-band sprawl for spare, plainspoken songs about grief and resolve. It's Woods at their most overtly political without losing the warm haze of their sound.
albums.lineage: A stripped-back turn within the Woods catalog, closer in mood to their early folk records than the jam-heavy mid-2010s run.

albums.label: Keeled Scales
albums.description: Mat Davidson's twain project sets a high, keening voice against loose, fingerpicked country-folk with occasional bursts of full-band warmth. It's intimate cosmic country, closer to a campfire than a road trip.
albums.lineage: Davidson's songwriting sounds indebted to Gram Parsons-style cosmic country and old-time singing, filtered through a DIY, small-label folk scene.

albums.label: Sacred Bones
albums.description: A more polished, radio-scaled record than Love, mixing McMahon's drawled vocals with warmer production, occasional synths, and mid-tempo grooves that borrow as much from classic rock as from psych-folk. Songs draw obliquely on McMahon's own family history and the pressures of masculinity. It suits listeners who want hypnotic rock with a surfer's easy momentum.
albums.lineage: Extends the breezy, classic-rock-informed direction of Love into a fuller studio sound that sounds akin to the Cosmic American Music revival.

albums.label: Jagjaguwar
albums.description: Max Clarke's first full-length as Cut Worms leans on ringing, Everly Brothers-style harmonies and simple, twangy guitar figures played at an unhurried country-pop tempo. It is a warm, sunny record that wears its 1960s and '70s country-rock influences openly without pastiche. Clarke's plainspoken songwriting keeps the mood breezy even when the lyrics turn wistful.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to Everly Brothers harmony singing and 1960s country-pop and country-rock, filtered through a Brooklyn DIY-pop sensibility.

albums.label: Silver Current Records
albums.description: Howlin Rain's long-form rock at its most confident, with harmonized lead guitars, anthemic choruses, and extended solos in the mode of the Dead's live improvisation. Crazy Horse-style fuzz and rolling mid-tempo grooves give the songs a road-worn, 1970s swagger. It suits listeners who want big classic-rock guitar with room to stretch.
albums.lineage: Sounds like a full expression of Grateful Dead- and Crazy Horse-style extended-jam songwriting.

albums.label: Mexican Summer
albums.description: Williamson's Mexican Summer debut sets her plainspoken, drawling voice against loose, twangy full-band arrangements, a step up in scale from her earlier, sparer albums. Songs move between hushed acoustic passages and warmer country-rock breeze, dealing frankly with desire, loneliness, and desert landscapes. It suits listeners who like intimate songwriting with a hazy, wide-open feel.
albums.lineage: Moves Williamson's earlier lo-fi folk toward a fuller country-rock sound that sounds indebted to Laurel Canyon; she later formed Plains with Katie Crutchfield.

albums.label: Bella Union
albums.description: A more synth-laced, polished record than Wilson's first two albums, though still built around long, winding guitar passages and breezy tempos. Its slicker, 1980s-tinged studio sound leans toward widescreen soft rock. It suits listeners who like lush, headphone-friendly production over rootsy grit.
albums.lineage: Shows Wilson's Laurel Canyon revivalism absorbing polished synth-rock textures, sounding akin to 1980s Pink Floyd-style studio rock without abandoning its cosmic foundation.

albums.label: Scissor Tail / Spinster
albums.description: Rosali Middleman's early solo record pairs plainspoken, deceptively simple songwriting with restrained electric-guitar backing, patient rather than showy. It sets the template for her later work with David Nance's Mowed Sound band: songs that unravel slowly, revealing more with repeat listens.
albums.lineage: Rooted in the Philadelphia DIY folk scene, laying groundwork for her later collaborations with Nebraska's Mowed Sound band on No Medium and Bite Down.

albums.label: Dead Oceans
albums.description: A deliberately harder-to-parse record than Walker's earlier Fahey-descended guitar albums, Deafman Glance buries his songwriting under synths, warped studio effects and loose improvisational playing from Chicago's experimental scene. Songs like 'In Castle Dome' drift and fracture rather than resolve, for listeners who like folk-rock with a free-jazz streak.
albums.lineage: Walker's most experimental studio record, pulling his American Primitive guitar roots into Chicago's free-improv and noise scene.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: A short, direct opening statement from Sean Thompson's project, built on Telecaster twang, a relaxed drawl, and a small backing band of drums, keys and bass. The songs lean on road-song imagery and breezy tempos. It suits listeners who like modest, well-played Nashville country rock.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to the 2010s Nashville DIY country-rock scene and its 1970s cosmic-country touchstones.

albums.label: Psychic Hotline
albums.description: Ryan Gustafson's main project, backed here by James Wallace (Skyway Man) and Molly Sarle (Mountain Man), mixes fingerpicked guitar and banjo with warm full-band arrangements. It is patient, plainspoken songwriting rooted in life on the road and in the North Carolina mountains.
albums.lineage: Gustafson has played guitar with Hiss Golden Messenger and shares members with Skyway Man, tying this record into the wider Asheville/Nashville cosmic-country web.

albums.label: Tiny Engines
albums.description: A synth-washed haze of guitar rock drawing openly on Springsteen and the War on Drugs, Yolk in the Fur is where Wild Pink's widescreen, heartland-indebted sound came into focus. It's warmer and more melodic than the debut while keeping its DIY scale.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to Springsteen's heartland rock and the War on Drugs' synth-guitar sound, filtered through a smaller-scale indie band.

albums.label: ANTI-
albums.description: A more exploratory record than Mangy Love, stretching several songs into long, Dead-like instrumental passages built on interlocking guitar lines. McCombs' deadpan, riddling lyrics stay intact even as the band jams out around them. It suits listeners who like their songwriting patient and their guitar playing unhurried.
albums.lineage: Sounds the most indebted to Grateful Dead-style long-form guitar jamming of any McCombs record, placing it alongside the 2010s cosmic-rock revival.

albums.label: Captured Tracks
albums.description: Cohen's self-titled third album keeps his mumbled, half-buried vocal style but opens the arrangements up with more keyboard and synth color. The tempos stay slow and breezy, and the mood remains warm rather than melancholy. It suits listeners who like soft-focus, gently psychedelic pop.
albums.lineage: Continues Cohen's subdued psychedelic pop, which sounds indebted to Laurel Canyon songwriting as much as to the art-pop of his former band Deerhoof.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: A prolific New Jersey guitar band named for a certain Dead guitarist, this album is built around long, twin-guitar jams that move between fuzzed-out heaviness and lighter, twangy interplay. Songs regularly stretch past seven minutes, foregrounding improvisation over verse-chorus structure. It is one of the clearest examples of the 2010s Dead-revival guitar-band sound.
albums.lineage: Directly channels the Grateful Dead's twin-guitar jam vocabulary, alongside peers like Ryley Walker and Endless Boogie in the 2010s psych-jam revival.

albums.label: Alive Naturalsound Records
albums.description: A laid-back homage to '70s Topanga Canyon and Marin County sounds from a band built around former Beachwood Sparks members: jangly, country-tinged FM rock full of easy harmonies. Warm guitars and unhurried tempos make it sound like a lost mid-'70s radio record. It suits listeners who like breezy, sun-bleached country rock.
albums.lineage: Formed by Beachwood Sparks' Brent Rademaker, directly continuing that band's cosmic-country line.

albums.label: Merge
albums.description: A more expansive record that stretches Hiss Golden Messenger's country-soul into longer, more atmospheric arrangements. Themes of self-doubt, depression, and endurance run through the lyrics, delivered over some of the band's most layered playing. It suits listeners who like their Americana patient, textured, and emotionally frank.
albums.lineage: Expands the Merge-era country-soul sound with a more atmospheric, layered production that sounds akin to the 2010s indie-Americana of peers like Bon Iver's circle.

albums.label: New West Records
albums.description: A fuller-band record than The Siren's Song, with more electric guitar interplay and a breezier tempo, while keeping the duo's plainspoken, old-timey vocal delivery. It leans further from strict folk revivalism toward a country-rock sound. It suits listeners who want traditional-minded songs with a warm electric band behind them.
albums.lineage: Extends Kacy & Clayton's move from folk repertoire toward a country-rock sound akin to Laurel Canyon.

albums.label: Dead Oceans
albums.description: A sprawling double-length song cycle about religion and mortality, built around piano, horns and gospel-adjacent backing vocals rather than guitar. It's Morby's most ambitious, least twangy record, but its questing, plainspoken spirituality keeps it in the Cosmic American Music lineage.
albums.lineage: Extends Morby's widescreen Dead Oceans period into full song-cycle territory, echoing the loose spiritual searching of the Grateful Dead's American Beauty-era songwriting.

albums.label: Keeled Scales
albums.description: Desert-toned cosmic country: reverb-heavy pedal steel, loping tempos and Shane Renfro's high, reedy voice drifting over slow-building arrangements. The songs take their time, letting guitars and steel smear into a warm, dusty haze. It suits listeners who want country rock with a psychedelic, heat-shimmer feel.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to Gram Parsons-style country rock filtered through desert psychedelia, akin to 2010s cosmic-country revivalists like Promised Land Sound and twain.

albums.label: Thrill Jockey
albums.description: Ripley Johnson's (Wooden Shjips, Moon Duo) country-rock project debuts with warm, unhurried songs built on layered acoustic and electric guitars and pedal steel. It trades Wooden Shjips' krautrock drone for a direct, breezy homage to 1970s country rock.
albums.lineage: Grew directly out of Johnson's psych-rock work in Wooden Shjips and Moon Duo, redirected toward country rock that sounds indebted to Gram Parsons and the Grateful Dead.

albums.label: Matador
albums.description: A more melancholy, string-touched record made in the wake of his father's death, The Unseen in Between trades some of the road-song sprawl for tighter, more classically-structured songs. It's Gunn's most direct singer-songwriter statement to date.
albums.lineage: Continues Gunn's Matador run with a turn toward orchestrated, personal songwriting rather than pure jam-length guitar pieces.

albums.album: The Congress of Teddy and The Rough Riders
albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: A Dead-inspired, psychedelic-twang debut from a Nashville band, mixing rowdy garage energy with pedal steel and guitar interplay. It has the loose, live-in-the-room feel of a band raised on both punk and country. It suits listeners who want road songs played loud and loose.
albums.lineage: Sounds akin to Nashville's 2010s DIY country-rock scene, with guitar interplay indebted to the Grateful Dead.

albums.label: Keeled Scales
albums.description: A warmer, more full-band twain record than its predecessors, still built around Davidson's reedy tenor but adding lightly psychedelic guitar textures and looser tempos. It keeps the intimacy of the earlier records while opening the windows a little, suited to slow afternoon listening.
albums.lineage: Continues the sound of Rare Feeling with a slightly fuller studio palette, still indebted to cosmic country.

albums.label: Arrowhawk Records
albums.description: A brighter, more classic-rock-structured record than I Hear You, New Petal Instants sounds like the Traveling Wilburys reimagined by Meat Puppets and Wilco, with cleaner hooks under the still-present fuzz. It's the band easing off pure noise toward actual songcraft.
albums.lineage: Shows Arbor Labor Union moving from distortion-first jamming toward more structured songs that sound indebted to Dead- and Wilburys-style country rock.

albums.label: Rhino Entertainment
albums.description: Formed by the late Neal Casal to play set-break music for the Grateful Dead's 2015 Fare Thee Well concerts before becoming its own band, this self-titled third LP pushes the instrumental jam group toward a groovier, cosmic-disco direction. It's an all-instrumental record that wears its Dead pedigree (bassist Dan Horne also plays in Beachwood Sparks) openly.
albums.lineage: Descends directly from the Grateful Dead's own jam vocabulary, connected to the wider LA cosmic-country scene through shared musicians like Dan Horne.

albums.label: Jagjaguwar
albums.description: A double album that widens Cut Worms' sound with brighter production and more layered harmonies while keeping the same easy country-pop tempos. Clarke's songwriting stays plain and melodic, closer to classic AM radio than to twang-rock swagger. It is the most expansive record in his catalog.
albums.lineage: Extends the buttery, harmony-driven sound of Hollow Ground, which sounds indebted to the Everly Brothers and Laurel Canyon pop, into a longer, more varied set.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: A tighter, more song-focused record than Cosmic Cash, though still anchored by extended guitar interplay between the band's two lead players. Tempos loosen into breezier, more melodic territory in places, without giving up the long jams entirely. It shows the band refining rather than abandoning their Dead-indebted approach.
albums.lineage: The band's name nods to Jerry Garcia, and its dual-guitar jamming sounds indebted to the Grateful Dead.

albums.label: Mexican Summer
albums.description: A patient, spacious record built around Williamson's low, unhurried voice and finger-picked, pedal-steel-laced arrangements. It trades the rawer edges of Cosmic Wink for a smoother, more mystical take on desert country-rock. Themes of self-possession and desire run through its longer, breezier songs.
albums.lineage: Continues Williamson's Mexican Summer-era cosmic country, which sounds indebted to Gram Parsons and Laurel Canyon; she later formed Plains with Katie Crutchfield.

albums.label: BMG
albums.description: This album pulls Wilson's sound closest to straight country, adding fiddle and pedal steel to his usual breezy, long-form guitar writing. It is a warmer, more rootsy record than Rare Birds, closer in spirit to Gentle Spirit. It suits listeners who want country rock with a stoned, unhurried glow.
albums.lineage: Brings Wilson's Laurel Canyon revivalism back toward country rock, sounding indebted to Gram Parsons and Nashville session-style picking.

albums.label: Dead Oceans
albums.description: Recorded largely alone at home after Morby moved back to Kansas City, this is his most spare, plainspoken record, built on finger-picked guitar, harmonica, and unhurried tempos. It trades the fuller band arrangements of his Los Angeles-era work for a hushed, small-town Midwestern feel. Reviewers linked its plainness to Springsteen's Nebraska as much as to cosmic country.
albums.lineage: A stripped-down turn in Morby's catalog that still carries the breezy, Dead- and Parsons-indebted guitar sensibility of his earlier band records.

albums.label: Yep Roc Records
albums.description: The duo's Yep Roc debut sharpens the songwriting while keeping the same easygoing intertwined-guitar sound, clearly steeped in the Flying Burrito Brothers and classic California country rock. It is warmer and more fully arranged than their debut, without losing its front-porch intimacy.
albums.lineage: Continues Mapache's California country-rock sound, which sounds indebted to Laurel Canyon and the Flying Burrito Brothers.

albums.label: Thrill Jockey
albums.description: The second Rose City Band album widens the sound with fuller arrangements and a sunnier, more anthemic set of songs, still anchored by Johnson's laconic voice and pedal steel. It plays like a long summer drive record, patient and glowing rather than showy.
albums.lineage: Expands on the debut's template, which sounds indebted to Gram Parsons and the Grateful Dead, with a fuller studio sound.

albums.label: Tompkins Square
albums.base: Los Angeles, CA (via Salt Lake City)
albums.description: Burton's debut LP pairs a high, Roy Orbison-like wail with moody, echo-laden country-rock production. Fingerpicked guitar and a hushed drawl give it an old, lonesome feel that plays as timeless rather than retro. It suits listeners who like crooned, reverb-soaked heartbreak songs.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to Roy Orbison's balladry and 1970s cosmic country, akin to the Woodsist circle's hazy country rock.

albums.label: Human Error Music
albums.description: Nashville pedal-steel sideman Spencer Cullum's debut as a bandleader is a sunny homage to '60s-'70s British and American folk-rock, cut with a cast of Music City players. It's less about his usual session role and more about letting his own songwriting lead, suited to fans of gentle, steel-soaked folk-rock.
albums.lineage: Grows out of Cullum's work as a Nashville session pedal-steel player, channeling his English folk-rock upbringing through the city's cosmic-country underground.

albums.label: Psychic Hotline
albums.description: Ryan Gustafson's most emotionally direct Dead Tongues album, reckoning with failed relationships and a religious upbringing over full-band arrangements. Harmonica and soft synths color breezy, storytelling folk rock. It suits listeners who want searching, spiritual songwriting with a warm band behind it.
albums.lineage: Sounds akin to the North Carolina cosmic folk-rock of peers like Hiss Golden Messenger.

albums.label: Atlantic
albums.description: A career-spanning live document assembled from years of shows, capturing how the band stretches its Dylan/Springsteen-via-Neil Young songs into extended, synth-lit jams on stage. It works as both a best-of and proof of the band's live reputation.
albums.lineage: Distills a decade of The War on Drugs' guitar rock, which sounds like Crazy Horse meeting motorik drive, into its most expansive, jam-lengthened form.

albums.label: Woodsist
albums.description: Woods work in synths and drum machines alongside their usual guitar interplay here, giving the record a hazier, more nocturnal feel than their jam-band-leaning mid-2010s albums. It's still built on Earl's falsetto and the band's loping, Dead-adjacent chord changes.
albums.lineage: Shows the Woodsist scene absorbing softer, synth-touched textures while keeping a backbone that sounds indebted to Crazy Horse and the Dead.

albums.label: Drag City
albums.description: A fuller-band, more overtly country-rock record than Hanson's debut, with pedal steel and long, winding guitar solos running through desert-toned songs. It leans into the sound of vintage Neil Young and Gene Clark records without straight pastiche. It suits listeners who want wide-open, sunburnt guitar music.
albums.lineage: Pulls Hanson's solo work closer to what sounds like classic Cosmic American Music in the Neil Young and Gene Clark mold.

albums.label: Merge
albums.description: A quieter, more reflective Hiss Golden Messenger record that folds subtle home-studio textures into the band's usual country-soul without losing the pedal steel and warm harmonies. The songs reckon with stillness, isolation, and small-town North Carolina life. It suits listeners who want gentle, unhurried roots music for late evenings.
albums.lineage: Shows Taylor bending his sound, which sounds rooted in the Grateful Dead and the Band, toward home-studio textures while keeping the same cosmic-country core.
key_tracks: Way Back in the Way Back
If It Comes in the Morning

albums.label: Woodsist
albums.description: Andrews leads this loose, sunny record of ramshackle country-folk. Ringing guitars and easygoing tempos carry conversational, unfussy songwriting throughout. It sits comfortably in the Woodsist label's twangy, DIY take on Laurel Canyon songwriting, for listeners who like their folk hazy and homespun.
albums.lineage: Sounds akin to the hazy, harmony-driven country-folk of Woodsist labelmates Woods.

albums.label: Mare Records
albums.description: Kazar's debut solo album is joyful, unhurried rock built on winding jams, pedal steel, and close harmonies. It mixes Band-style looseness with a glammy, playful pop streak. It suits listeners who want warm 1970s-leaning rock with a grin.
albums.lineage: Released on Kevin Morby's Mare Records imprint; its loose, harmony-rich rock sounds indebted to the Band and 1970s pop-rock.

albums.label: Innovative Leisure / Calico Discos
albums.description: The duo keeps refining their guitar-and-harmony formula, with intertwined acoustic guitars and close, easy vocals. It is short, warm and unpretentious, songs built for a porch or a campfire rather than a festival stage.
albums.lineage: A continuation of Mapache's California country-duo sound, which sounds indebted to the Everly Brothers and the Flying Burrito Brothers.

albums.label: Spinster Records
albums.description: Rosali's first collaboration with David Nance's Mowed Sound band opens up her songs into looser, more guitar-forward arrangements, closer to Neil Young or Yo La Tengo than singer-songwriter folk. Her plainspoken drawl rides warm Telecaster lines and harmonized guitars at easy tempos.
albums.lineage: Marks the start of her ongoing partnership with the Mowed Sound band, a key thread connecting Philadelphia and Omaha DIY scenes.

albums.label: Thrill Jockey
albums.description: A patient, groove-heavy record that leans further into the band's live-jam side, with extended guitar and pedal-steel interplay over motorik rhythms. It is psychedelic country rock for a long, stoned drive, trading drone-rock heaviness for open-prairie ease.
albums.lineage: Continues Johnson's arc from Wooden Shjips' drone-rock toward fully-formed cosmic country.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: A trip into '70s classic-rock territory, all chiming guitars, T-Rex stomp and Lou Reed-style breeziness. The band favors warmth and laid-back groove over polish, evoking the late-'60s and early-'70s golden era rather than throwback pastiche.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to Britfolk- and glam-inflected early-'70s classic rock, with a garage-rock looseness.

albums.label: Matador
albums.description: Other You folds subtle synth textures into Gunn's guitar-first sound without losing its unhurried, sun-bleached feel. Soft drums, layered guitars and his relaxed voice give it a hazy, meditative calm. It plays like a gentler sibling to Way Out Weather.
albums.lineage: A late-period Matador record that keeps Gunn's cosmic-country songwriting intact while widening its palette with electronics.

albums.label: Terrible Records
albums.description: Ben Schwab's Sylvie project trades the psych-pop of his Golden Daze work for spare, warm country-folk arrangements. It's a slight but gorgeous record of soft vocals, brushed drums and gentle guitar, for listeners who like their '70s revival hushed.
albums.lineage: A side project of Golden Daze's Ben Schwab, carrying that LA psych-pop scene toward softer '70s-style country-folk.

albums.label: Atlantic
albums.description: A slightly brighter, more direct record than its predecessors, with tighter songwriting and guest vocals from Lucius. Still built on the band's signature long crescendos and Telecaster shimmer, it is a comfortable, confident continuation rather than a reinvention.
albums.lineage: Continues the band's cosmic-Americana lineage into the 2020s, an established touchstone for younger heartland-adjacent songwriters.

albums.label: Royal Mountain Records
albums.description: Wild Pink's breakout record layers pedal steel and strings under John Ross's introspective, plainspoken lyrics, arriving at a lush, heartland-scaled sound. Mid-tempo songs build slowly to widescreen peaks, for listeners who want indie rock with a country sheen.
albums.lineage: Wild Pink's fullest realization of pedal-steel-dressed indie rock, sounding like a crossover point between heartland rock and the C1 twang scene.

albums.label: ANTI-
albums.description: This album keeps McCombs' warm, unhurried guitar-rock sound while turning toward more openly emotional lyrics about grief and love. The tempos stay breezy and the arrangements uncluttered, closer to Mangy Love than to Tip of the Sphere's jams. It is for listeners who want his songwriting at its gentlest.
albums.lineage: Continues McCombs' ANTI- era guitar rock; its softer edges sound indebted to classic Laurel Canyon songwriting.

albums.label: Fat Possum
albums.description: Loose Future opens Courtney Marie Andrews back up into full-band, '70s-flavored arrangements after the bare-bones Old Flowers, with buttery lead guitar and warm harmonies replacing the earlier record's silence. The mood is lighter and more hopeful, suited to listeners who like breezy, sunlit country rock.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to the country-rock/Cosmic American Music lineage, following her own path from stripped-down folk into the cosmic country revival.
key_tracks: These Are the Good Old Days

albums.label: Single Lock Records
albums.description: A more textured, golden-toned record than Putting On Airs, layering Rae's strong, unhurried voice over arrangements that borrow from 1970s AM radio without tipping into kitsch. Every arrangement stays tasteful and uncluttered, with pedal steel and close harmonies giving it a breezy, cosmic-country glow. It suits listeners who want warm, soft-focus country-folk.
albums.lineage: Extends Rae's Nashville country-folk into a sound akin to 1970s AM-radio soft rock and Cosmic American Music.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: New Jersey's Garcia Peoples keep working the dual-guitar-jam vein of their earlier records, all extended solos and interlocking leads in the spirit of the guitarist their name nods to. It's dense, riff-forward psych-jam rock built for headphones or a long drive.
albums.lineage: Takes its name from Jerry Garcia and sounds directly indebted to his lead style and the Dead's long-form jamming.

albums.label: Dead Oceans
albums.description: Sparked by an old photograph of his father found after a family health scare, this album is a warm, mid-tempo meditation on mortality and memory, built on breezy country-rock arrangements with pedal steel and horns. Recorded partly in Memphis, it draws on that city's soul and gospel history as much as on Laurel Canyon songwriting. It suits listeners who want reflective songs with a big, generous band sound.
albums.lineage: Continues Morby's move toward a fuller folk-rock and country sound that sounds indebted to Dylan, the Band, and Memphis soul; it was followed by the companion More Photographs (A Continuum).

albums.label: SPINSTER
albums.description: Microcosmos is a spacious cycle of cosmic country songs from Lou Turner, her warm, conversational voice finding humor and grace in small domestic moments. Its deadpan warmth recalls Silver Jews and Lambchop, for listeners who like country songs slow and wry.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to '70s singer-songwriters like Joni Mitchell, with touchstones in Bill Callahan and Silver Jews' wry, plainspoken style.

albums.label: Innovative Leisure / Calico Discos
albums.description: A long, generous set of earnest, classic songwriting built on intertwined acoustic guitars and close duo harmonies. It is an unpretentious road-trip record from a duo comfortable with letting songs breathe. It suits listeners who want easygoing California country-folk to play front to back.
albums.lineage: The most expansive entry in Mapache's catalog, extending their duo-harmony format across a longer set.

albums.label: Secretly Canadian
albums.description: Whitney's most ambitious record, grown from acoustic demos into full arrangements, folds synths and programmed textures into their usual horn-and-guitar warmth. It's a left-field stretch for the band without losing the easy melodicism and falsetto of the debut.
albums.lineage: Whitney's furthest reach from their country-soul debut, though still built on the same warm, horn-inflected songwriting core.

albums.label: Royal Mountain Records
albums.description: Written and recorded after John Ross's cancer diagnosis, ILYSM is a more inward, cathartic record than its predecessor, its heartland-scale arrangements now carrying real emotional weight. Synths, guitars and pedal steel swell around Ross's soft, conversational voice.
albums.lineage: A personal, health-crisis-driven turn within Wild Pink's pedal-steel-and-synth heartland sound.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: Gabe Birnbaum's band shares out lead vocals over extended, guitar-forward jams and replayable choruses. It is a generous, collaborative record built for a full band stretching out live. It suits listeners who like storytelling songs with big, harmonized guitar breaks.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to 1970s long-solo rock and New York indie songwriting.

albums.label: Woodsist / Mare
albums.description: St. Louis's second album opens up her stark debut into brighter, more orchestral arrangements of strings, piano and fingerpicked guitar. It trades the gritty apparitions of her first record for patient, present-tense contentment, sung in her low, unhurried voice.
albums.lineage: Connects directly to the Woodsist label that released her debut, and sounds of a piece with the West Coast singer-songwriter circle of Jess Williamson and Kacey Johansing.

albums.label: Sophomore Lounge
albums.description: Yonder is Arbor Labor Union's most introspective, nocturnal record, cleaner and more inward than the kaleidoscopic New Petal Instants but no less indebted to the Allmans and Neil Young. Unhurried guitar lines wind around each other at walking tempos, suited to late-night listening.
albums.lineage: A quieter turn within Arbor Labor Union's catalog that still sounds drawn from the same Dead/Allman Brothers well as their earlier fuzzed-out records.

albums.label: Drag City
albums.description: A provocatively titled record built around long guitar-solo epics, closer to Hanson's Wand side than his quieter solo debut. Country-rock tempos and pedal steel still anchor the songs even as the guitar playing stretches out at length. It suits listeners who want shredding that still feels warm and melodic.
albums.lineage: Reconnects Hanson's solo work to long-form guitar jamming that sounds indebted to the Dead and Crazy Horse.

albums.label: Jagjaguwar
albums.description: The self-titled album pares Cut Worms' sound back to a leaner, more direct country-pop. Melodies stay bright and hooky, riding on the same twangy, harmony-laden guitar interplay as his earlier work. It reads as a mid-career consolidation rather than a reinvention, for fans of sweet, retro-minded songcraft.
albums.lineage: Keeps Cut Worms in a country-pop vein that sounds indebted to the Everly Brothers and Gram Parsons, as across his whole catalog.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: Warm harmony vocals sit against loose, breezy guitar arrangements on this full-length. The songs move at an easy tempo somewhere between cosmic country and dream-pop, with fingerpicked acoustic lines and a gentle drawl. It suits listeners who like soft, sunlit harmony songwriting.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to Laurel Canyon-style harmony songwriting filtered through DIY self-release culture.

albums.label: Merge
albums.description: A relatively lean, upbeat record with brighter tempos and some of Taylor's most direct choruses. Pedal steel and harmony vocals sit up front, in keeping with the buttery, breezy sound that defines his Merge catalog. It suits fans who want Hiss Golden Messenger at its most sunny and hook-driven.
albums.lineage: A late-period return to a communal, road-band version of Hiss Golden Messenger's cosmic country, sounding indebted to the Band and Grateful Dead country rock.

albums.label: Arrowhawk Records
albums.description: Silverstein alternates expansive pedal-steel-laced instrumentals with songs sung in a delivery pitched between Bill Callahan's deadpan and Kurt Vile's drift. It's cosmic country in the vein of Beachwood Sparks and Silver Jews, slow and sunlit.
albums.lineage: Sounds of a piece with the Pacific Northwest cosmic-country instrumentalists around Rose City Band, sharing their pedal-steel drift.

albums.label: Mexican Summer
albums.description: Williamson's most fully country-identified record, with pedal steel, warm harmonies, and road-song imagery throughout. It works through the end of one relationship and the start of another with plainspoken directness, her voice sitting close and unhurried over two-step and ballad tempos. It suits listeners who want classic country feeling from an indie-bred songwriter.
albums.lineage: Brings Williamson's cosmic-country sound closest to what sounds like Gram Parsons and outlaw-country roots; she also records with Katie Crutchfield as Plains.

albums.label: Night Bloom Records
albums.description: A gentle, warmly produced set of songs about distance and homecoming, Year Away favors soft-focus folk-pop arrangements over the twangier end of the C6 sound. It's closer to a hushed Laurel Canyon lullaby than a jam band, for listeners who want close harmonies and patient tempos.
albums.lineage: Sounds of a piece with the West Coast singer-songwriter circle around Anna St. Louis and Jess Williamson, sharing their soft-focus Laurel Canyon warmth.

albums.label: Innovative Leisure / Calico Discos
albums.description: A relaxed set that continues the duo's front-porch harmony sound with a slightly fuller band arrangement. Intertwined acoustic guitars and unhurried tempos keep the mood warm and easy. It suits listeners who like classic California country rock played with gentle sincerity.
albums.lineage: Extends Mapache's ongoing homage to what sounds like Flying Burrito Brothers-style California country rock.

albums.label: Kill Rock Stars
albums.description: Davis's harp anchors a full-band record that weaves '60s pop melodies, psychedelia and driving folk rock. Steel guitar and close harmonies give it a country-rock backbone, and the band's interplay recalls Fleetwood Mac at their most collaborative. It suits listeners who want sunny, harmony-rich rock with a cosmic tilt.
albums.lineage: Leans into a harmony-driven jam-pop sound that sounds akin to the Grateful Dead's gentler side and Fleetwood Mac.

albums.label: Thrill Jockey
albums.description: A tighter, hookier set than its predecessors, with the band sounding fully locked in. Pedal steel and harmonized guitars balance sunlit pop songcraft with room to stretch out at breezy, anthemic tempos. It suits listeners who want cosmic country at its most concise and summery.
albums.lineage: Part of Rose City Band's steady evolution of a cosmic-country template that sounds indebted to Gram Parsons and the Grateful Dead.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: Mapache's Sam Blasucci steps out solo, trading intertwined acoustic guitars for piano and writing autobiographical songs about settling into adult life. Close harmonies and hushed, breezy arrangements keep it intimate. It suits listeners who like gentle, diaristic singer-songwriter records.
albums.lineage: A solo detour from Blasucci's work in the California country duo Mapache.

albums.label: Partisan Records
albums.description: Burton's second album trades some of I Can Go With You's stark folk for fuller, Laurel Canyon-style arrangements, with pedal steel and strings framing his warm, unhurried baritone. It's gentler and more polished than the debut without losing its plainspoken sadness.
albums.lineage: Moves Burton from the Tompkins Square country-folk revival roster to Partisan, with a sound indebted to '70s LA soft country rock.

albums.album: Flight of the Long Distance Healer
albums.label: Mama Bird Recording Co.
albums.description: James Wallace's kaleidoscopic project mixes piano-led psychedelic rock with dense, spacey arrangements and strings. Opaque, mystic lyrics sit over swampy, soulful, gospel-tinged production. It suits listeners who want anthemic, cosmic songwriting with a spiritual bent.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to 1970s gospel-tinged psychedelic rock and cosmic country.

albums.label: Full Time Hobby
albums.description: Cullum's second Coin Collection album pulls further from his English folk-rock reference points toward stranger, more subconscious songwriting, with layered arrangements from Nashville players. It keeps the pedal-steel-led warmth while hiding its influences further from view.
albums.lineage: A step deeper into Nashville's instrumentalist underground, still rooted in Cullum's pedal-steel session background.
key_tracks: What a Waste of an Echo

albums.label: Woodsist
albums.description: Woods' 2023 album settles into a warm, unhurried guitar-band sound full of long fades, loops and gently interlocking leads. Two decades in, it plays like a settled, confident restatement of what the band and the Woodsist label have stood for. It suits listeners who like hazy, patient psych-folk.
albums.lineage: A late-career synthesis of the Woods catalog, still released on Jeremy Earl's own Woodsist label, whose scene it sounds central to.
key_tracks: Where Do You Go When You Dream

albums.label: Curation
albums.description: The 2000s cosmic-country revivalists' first album in over a decade, mixing pedal-steel-laced country rock with the band's longtime dreamy, harmony-driven sound. The songs drift at easy tempos with jangling guitars and soft group vocals. It is a warm late-career return for fans of their early records.
albums.lineage: A late-career return from one of the foundational 2000s cosmic-country revival bands (C6); their sound is indebted to V21 country rock and the Paisley Underground's jangle.

albums.label: Hardly Art
albums.description: Made with contributions from Jeff Parker and Josh Johnson, this record keeps Cohen's subdued psychedelia while adding jazzier color and understated hooks. It moves through hazy, mysterious moods without ever raising its volume. It marked Cohen's move from Captured Tracks to Hardly Art.
albums.lineage: Extends Cohen's breezy, Laurel Canyon-adjacent pop songwriting into jazzier arrangements, deepening a catalog that has quietly run in parallel to the wider cosmic-country revival.

albums.label: New West Records
albums.description: Color Green's second album is a meditation on grief and clarity delivered through loose, live-feeling jams, from the hush of '5:08' to the sprawling 'Kick the Bucket.' Guitars trade lines and voices stack into harmonies the way a band that treats every gig as improvisation would.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to '60s SoCal folk-rock and the Dead/Allmans jam vocabulary, delivered with a live-band looseness.

albums.label: Western Vinyl
albums.description: Wilder Maker frontman Gabriel Birnbaum's solo album mines character studies of quiet desperation over lush, psychedelic-tinged folk-rock, closer to Paul Simon's narrative songcraft than his main band's more experimental side. It's a mature, unhurried record built on empathetic detail.
albums.lineage: A solo outlet for the Wilder Maker frontman that leans further into plainspoken, character-driven folk-rock storytelling.

albums.label: House Band (self-released)
albums.description: A debut LP from a loose LA collective, Aventurine spreads out into sprawling, heady grooves that recall electric-era Miles Davis and Can as much as the Dead. Its jam-length instrumental patience and synth textures put it at the far cosmic edge of this lane.
albums.lineage: Sounds like the cosmic-jam end of the scene stretched into krautrock and fusion territory, indebted to Can and electric Miles as much as the Dead.

albums.album: Songs From A Thousand Frames Of Mind
albums.label: Ghostly International
albums.description: Kate Bollinger's kaleidoscopic full-length debut ranges from homespun folk songs to warmly psychedelic rock. Her airy soprano and jazzy, organic arrangements give it a Laurel Canyon-adjacent glow.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to Françoise Hardy, the Velvet Underground and Teenage Fanclub as much as country, landing at the pop-facing edge of this lane's '70s revival strand.

albums.label: Perpetual Doom
albums.description: Baggett makes crunchy, warm Crazy Horse-style rock here, all snaking guitar solos and B3 organ. It sits comfortably alongside the mellower, jam-friendly end of this lane, for listeners who like their fuzz relaxed.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to Crazy Horse's loose guitar rock, filtered through the relaxed sensibility of West Coast lo-fi songwriters like Little Wings.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: Sam Cantor's Chicago band mixes alt-country songwriting with adventurous, Dead-like guitar theatrics and pedal steel. Storytelling lyrics sit over harmonized guitars that stretch out without losing the songs. It suits listeners who want Midwestern alt-country with a cosmic streak.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to Grateful Dead and Crazy Horse guitar playing filtered through Midwestern alt-country songwriting.

albums.label: Merge Records
albums.description: Rosali's Merge Records debut, again with Nance's Mowed Sound band, elaborates elliptical folk songs into full-bodied guitar rock reminiscent of Yo La Tengo or Neil Young. Her voice carries a mesmerizing pull in the vein of Sandy Denny or Will Oldham, over long solos and harmonized guitars.
albums.lineage: The full flowering of her Mowed Sound collaboration, moving her from DIY folk circles onto a larger indie label.

albums.label: Flying Cloud Recordings
albums.description: Sam Owens's fourth album as Sam Evian chases a warm, early-1970s Laurel Canyon feel across loose, groove-driven songs. Soft vocals, relaxed tempos and a live-band warmth make it for listeners who like cosmic-country-tinged soft rock.
albums.lineage: A Catskills singer-songwriter whose sound is indebted to the Laurel Canyon and Gram Parsons-adjacent cosmic-country lineage.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: An Auckland quartet's sophomore LP mixes desert twang, brooding psych atmospherics and country phrasing into immersive, dynamically wide-ranging arrangements. It swings between rowdy and delicate, for listeners who like cosmic country with a darker, more atmospheric edge.
albums.lineage: Part of a small but growing Antipodean cosmic-country scene taking the Dead/Beachwood Sparks lineage outside the US.

albums.label: Appalachia Record Co. / Cleft Music
albums.description: Down Home is a Dead-inspired set of psychedelic twang, warm, loose and collaborative in feel. Its front-porch take on cosmic country favors easy grooves, harmonies and winding guitar over polish.
albums.lineage: Sounds of a piece with Nashville's Dead-indebted country-rock scene around acts like Coin Collection and Rich Ruth.

albums.label: Super High Quality Records
albums.description: A follow-up live set drawn from the I Don't Live Here Anymore tour, again showing how songs built in the studio around layered synths and guitar loops unfurl even longer on stage. Adam Granduciel's guitar solos get plenty of room to stretch.
albums.lineage: Second entry in the Live Drugs series, continuing the band's arena-scale guitar rock, which sounds indebted to Crazy Horse and Dylan, in concert form.

albums.label: Spoilsport Records / Earth Libraries
albums.description: Dylan Young's Way Dynamic studies mellow '70s songwriting in the Carole King, Jackson Browne, Harry Nilsson and Todd Rundgren mode, dressed in baroque-pop string arrangements. It is playful and melodic rather than jam-heavy, closer to chamber-pop revivalism than Dead-style sprawl.
albums.lineage: Young also leads the Melbourne band Cool Sounds; here he channels what sounds like '70s Laurel Canyon songcraft into a minimalist folk-pop frame.

albums.label: Fire Talk
albums.description: Wild Pink's fifth album trades some of ILYSM's studio polish for a rougher, heavier rock palette. The title track is a fist-raising ode to moving on, with louder guitars and a more direct band sound than before.
albums.lineage: Wild Pink's rawest, most rock-forward record to date, still carrying the heartland/pedal-steel DNA of their Royal Mountain years.

albums.label: Saddle Creek
albums.description: Ada Lea's third album is her most playful and breezy, trading the moodier indie rock of her earlier records for '70s Laurel Canyon folk warmth and slice-of-life humor under a Dylan-borrowed title. Alexandra Levy's plainspoken voice carries loose, sun-drenched arrangements built for driving.
albums.lineage: Sounds like a late turn toward Cosmic American Music textures for a Montreal songwriter previously closer to art-rock; it sits alongside Kate Bollinger and Courtney Marie Andrews' own Laurel Canyon-leaning records in this lane.

albums.label: Sophomore Lounge
albums.description: A short follow-up EP to Yonder that keeps the same winding, left-field guitar grooves and Dead-indebted chord changes in a tighter package. The playing is crunchy and unpredictable, a quick fix for fans of the band's longer records.
albums.lineage: A compact continuation of Arbor Labor Union's post-Yonder sound, still sounding indebted to the Dead/Allman Brothers vein.

albums.label: Domino
albums.description: Interior Live Oak returns to the more economical song structures of McCombs' earlier records while keeping his prime-era wit and melodic ease. Relaxed guitars and his low, conversational voice give it a warm, unhurried feel. It's a hopeful, clarifying record from an artist who's spent two decades circling extremes.
albums.lineage: Marks McCombs' return to Domino after his ANTI- Records albums, circling back to his earlier songwriting style.

albums.label: Drag City
albums.description: A full swerve from Hanson's scorching guitar-rock records into piano-led, orchestral balladry in the Nashville Sound mold, carrying sarcastic, well-built songs. It keeps the breezy tempos of his earlier work while trading long solos for lusher, more classic-country arrangement. It is his most stylistically surprising solo record, for fans of wry, lushly dressed songcraft.
albums.lineage: Bends Hanson's solo catalog toward orchestration that sounds indebted to the classic Nashville Sound.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: A self-released Los Angeles record built on warm, breezy guitar interplay and easygoing tempos in the Dead-revival mode. The songwriting stays understated rather than showy, favoring feel over flash.
albums.lineage: Part of the same self-released, Dead-indebted West Coast guitar-band underground as Garcia Peoples and Cass McCombs' looser records.

albums.label: Full Time Hobby
albums.description: This self-titled record blends Radiohead-style atmospherics with Nilsson-esque psychedelic pop and woozy, pub-rock-adjacent Americana. Synths and pedal steel drift together at breezy, hushed tempos. It suits listeners who like country textures pushed into dreamy, experimental pop.
albums.lineage: Sounds akin to Nashville's instrumentalist-led cosmic country scene (Rich Ruth, Spencer Cullum), taken in a more song-based, psychedelic-pop direction.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: Glyders' second full-length was flagged by Josh Terry as a forthcoming record to watch, continuing the duo's mix of breezy, harmony-driven guitar pop and cosmic-country tempos. It builds on Maria's Hunt with slightly fuller, more anthemic arrangements. The band remains a self-released Chicago project more than a decade after forming.
albums.lineage: Continues Glyders' Laurel Canyon-indebted harmony songwriting within Chicago's independent DIY scene.

albums.label: Congrats Records
albums.description: Cohen's fourth album, made with partner and producer Sam Evian at their Catskills studio Flying Cloud, is a hazy collage of memory built from years of home recording. Its soft-focus folk-pop favors atmosphere over hooks, with hushed vocals floating over gentle acoustic and keyboard textures.
albums.lineage: Grows out of the Flying Cloud/Sam Evian Catskills recording circle, the upstate-New York studio and label run by her partner.

albums.label: Congrats Records
albums.description: Kazar's second solo LP is cozy, conversational folk-rock in a New Morning and Wings register, with pedal steel and fiddle threading through warm, unhurried songs about everyday intimacy. It suits listeners who like homey, melodic 1970s-style songcraft.
albums.lineage: Continues Kazar's post-Due North songwriting in a mode that sounds indebted to early-'70s Dylan and Paul McCartney.

albums.label: Thrill Jockey
albums.description: Johnson's most emotionally shadowed Rose City Band record, letting a melancholy undertone sit alongside the band's usual sun-kissed grooves. Pedal steel remains the glinting through-line, with long, harmonized guitar solos stretching over relaxed tempos. It suits listeners who like their cosmic country with a dusk-colored edge.
albums.lineage: The latest chapter in Johnson's long arc from Wooden Shjips/Moon Duo psych-drone to widescreen cosmic country.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: An airy, piano-led set that trades some of Off My Stars' folk directness for a more sophisticated pop croon. Tasteful rather than showy, it continues Blasucci's move away from Mapache's guitar-forward sound.
albums.lineage: Follows Off My Stars in the solo evolution of Mapache member Blasucci away from the duo format.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: Thompson's debut full-band LP trades some of his earlier twang for exploratory, cosmic territory, with easygoing songs about country living and long drives. It is a step forward from the project's 2022 self-titled EP, built around his guitar playing and loose, jam-friendly arrangements.
albums.lineage: Builds on Thompson's Nashville session career and his earlier Weird Ears EPs into a fuller cosmic-country-jam statement.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: An instrumental trio's debut built from long-drive jamming with pedal steel, guitar, and synths. It luxuriates in kosmische, ambient and jazz-fusion textures rather than song structure, Dead-adjacent in spirit but closer to Alice Coltrane or Ashra in execution. It suits listeners who want slow, glowing instrumental music.
albums.lineage: Sounds akin to Nashville's instrumentalist-led cosmic country, with debts to kosmische and spiritual jazz.

albums.label: Curation Records
albums.description: A playful cosmic-pop record that sits somewhere between New Riders of the Purple Sage and the Clientele, released on the Curation label. Pedal steel from Luke Schneider and flute from Rex Gregory widen the band's palette beyond their glammier debut.
albums.lineage: Deepens Silver Synthetic's turn from garage punk toward cosmic country, aligning them with the Curation Records/Beachwood Sparks lineage.

albums.label: Secretly Canadian
albums.description: A return to fuller, more assured songwriting after SPARK's detour into synths, Small Talk puts Whitney's warm country-soul back at the center. The horns and Julien Ehrlich's falsetto are still the core of the sound, delivered with more confidence and a gentle pedal-steel sheen.
albums.lineage: A confident late-career synthesis of Whitney's country-soul debut and their more expansive mid-period records.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: A brief, folk-based debut built on plucked strings and a mallet-driven pulse, with playful, transcendental lyrics floating over spare, exploratory arrangements. The mood is spectral and cosmic, a little spooky despite its lullaby-like gentleness. It suits listeners who want hushed, spiritual folk-pop to sink into.
albums.lineage: A hushed, folk-song take on cosmic music that sounds closer to Vashti Bunyan than to full-band jam-rock.

albums.label: Gar Hole Records
albums.description: Angela Autumn folds American folk and bluegrass roots into a hybridized, big-sounding record on Believer, blending indie, psychedelia and gothic country. Twangy picking sits under heavy, reverb-washed production. It suits listeners who like old-time roots pushed toward the psychedelic.
albums.lineage: Sounds rooted in Appalachian old-time and bluegrass tradition, recast through the 2020s cosmic-country revival's bigger, more psychedelic production.

albums.label: Loose Future Records
albums.description: Valentine finds Courtney Marie Andrews leaning further into ornate, Laurel Canyon-styled folk, her Ronstadt-range voice wrapped in ethereal harmonies and a warm, '70s Nashville palette. Slow-rolling piano, pedal steel and brushed drums keep it intimate, for fans of classic country-folk heartbreak.
